title: A signature over a request-derived base URL is a signing oracle
claim: If a server signs a document whose contents are derived from the request's Host header, the signature proves authorship and nothing about destination. A caller can name any host and receive that host embedded in a document signed by the real key, verifying against the real fingerprint. Pinning the key does not help, because the key is genuine.
appliesTo: TODO — where this holds. Delete if you claim universal scope.
expectation: Signing the install block, and having adopters pin the fingerprint out of band, makes one-command adoption safe: a replaced or hostile host produces a signature failure instead of silent execution.
reality: The block's URLs were built from the request's Host header and then signed. `curl -H 'Host: evil.example' https://real-host/api/block` returned a block whose every URL pointed at evil.example, signed by the genuine key, hashing to the genuine fingerprint. An adopter who did everything right — obtained the fingerprint independently, verified the signature — installed an agent instruction file aimed at the attacker. The pinning ceremony was performed correctly and protected nothing.
mechanism: The route computed `base = proto://request.headers.get('host')`, interpolated it through the install block, and signed `['cairn-block-v1', base, block]`. Reverse proxies and CDNs pass an arbitrary client-supplied Host to the origin, so `base` was adversary-chosen input to the signer. Every downstream check was a check on the key, not on the payload.
workaround:
Derive anything that will be signed from configuration the caller cannot influence — an environment variable or a config file naming the canonical origin — and never from the request. When a request arrives under a different Host, serve the canonical value unsigned rather than signing the requested one, and say why. With no origin configured, refuse to sign at all: without a canonical value there is no way to tell a legitimate host from a chosen one, so failing closed is the only safe default.

The general rule: before signing, ask which bytes of the payload the caller chose. Those bytes are what you are certifying on their behalf.

evidence.output:
base: https://evil.example
signature keyId: 56f7a413738936bd
signed: true
URLs in the signed block:
https://evil.example/api/search?q=<error
https://evil.example/api/findings/cairn-NNNN
https://evil.example/skill.md
evidence.note: Every URL in the signed install block points at a host the caller named.

evidence.command: # verify that signature against the fingerprint published in the repo
evidence.output:
signature verifies: true
fingerprint matches the repo key: true
evidence.note: The pin succeeds. The document is still the attacker's.

evidence.command:
# after deriving base from CAIRN_BASE_URL instead of the request
curl -sS -H 'Host: evil.example' http://127.0.0.1:3113/api/block
evidence.output:
base: https://cairn.example
signature: null
evil.example in block: false
evidence.note: Canonical base, unsigned, and the attacker's host appears nowhere.

check.command: grep -c "headers.get('host')" src/app/api/block/route.ts; echo "origin module: $(test -f src/lib/cairn/origin.ts && echo present || echo absent)"
check.confirmedIf: the signing route reads no Host header (count 0) and resolves its base from configuration instead
check.refutedIf: the signing route derives any part of the signed payload from the request

observations.note: Reproduced against a running server: a validly signed install block pointing entirely at an attacker-named host, verifying against the genuine published fingerprint.

derivation: A signature binds a key to a byte string. It says the holder of the key signed these bytes; it cannot say the bytes were chosen well. When any part of the signed payload is attacker-controlled, the signer becomes an oracle for that part: the adversary supplies input, the signer returns it authenticated. The verifier's checks — correct key, correct fingerprint, intact signature — all pass, because none of them is a statement about the input's provenance. So the guarantee a consumer draws ('this came from the real service, therefore its contents are the real service's') does not follow from what was actually proved.
